messages.subject: best use of our testing time?
messages.subject_clean: best use of our testing time?
messages.body_plain:
Unit testing gives me a lot of time for reflection.

Summary
-----------------------------------

I feel we're missing the forest for the trees in testing.

Given our limited time budget, I think it would be better spent
with more functional specification and testing and less time
unit testing.

Example of Unit Testing Pain
------------------------------------

To plug the memory leak in softmax, I:

1.  first verified there was a leak writing a test and then looking
at the process in the Activity Monitor (Mac process monitor).

2.  fixed the leak by replacing "operator new" with "memalloc_.alloc".

3.  verified there was no longer a leak using the activity monitor.

Now the fun begins.

4.  I wrote e-mail to the mailing list asking how to test a memory leak.
As of 2.1.0, there was no testing at all that we aren't leaking memory.

5.  Ben suggested a Windows-incompatible test on memory, and given I
don't know how to do the same in Windows, I didn't look further.

6. Daniel suggested monitoring stack size, but the problem was that
the allocation wasn't happening on the stack, just on the heap, so
I couldn't use a simple stack size test.

7.  Instead, I wrote a new function in stack_alloc that monitors the
amount of memory allocated to Stan through memalloc_ instance.  But
that doesn't line up real well with memory requested through
stack_alloc::alloc due to unused bytes at the end of blocks.

8.  Then I had to go write a test for stack_alloc::bytes_allocated.  I had initially
wanted to track memory allocated from memalloc_, but that turns out
to be impossible given that we don't fill blocks or keep track of where
the memory went (nor do we need to!).

9.  Next, I went back and wrote a test for softmax that failed in the
old version and succeeded in the new version by printing out bytes
allocated in our current code.  The key here is that the memory should've been
allocated on this stack, not the general C++ heap.  This test is extremely brittle
and dependent on current data structure sizes and block size constants.  It will
have to be refiddled if we change the constants in stack_alloc or the data structures
in softmax.   (This is an example of the kinds of problem Michael anticipated and
we've already run into with the command-line tests.)

What I Should Have Done
-------------------------------------

To be properly modular, what I should've done was written a new
feature request for the bytes_allocated function, specified it, tested
it, then written the unit test for that.

Instead, I sloppily introduced a new public function in an unrelated part of
the memory allocation code simply to support tests.

At least I put it in a different commit, making sure all of the commits
passed all of our unit tests (a huge time sink for the computer, if not
for me).

Was it Worth it?
-----------------------------------

All of this testing took much much much longer than the fix itself and
involved the attention of at least three of our developers before the
fix and will require at least one developer's time to code review.
I think the fix took about five minutes and the unit testing about two hours,
including writing the new functions.

The end result is very brittle, and I'm not sure it's telling us anything
that looking at the activity monitor didn't tell me (other than that it's
automated, but as I mentioned above, that's likely to bite us later due to
its brittleness).

In this case, I think we could've just code reviewed the change and
gone with it.  But this brings up the next issue.

Subjective Nature of When Enough is Enough
------------------------------------------------

Another problem I see is that how much testing to do is a judgment call.
I may trust myself and code reviewers in situations like this one that
seem totally obvious to me.  But are they totally obvious?  It's very subjective,
and my guess is that we're all overconfident in our fixes, exactly the
problem that unit testing is trying to mitigate.

I'm not sure any of us understand Daniel's line between
enough and not-enough testing.  (I'm only picking out Daniel because he's
been driving this process and we put him in charge of gatekeeping merges a
few meetings ago.)

Time Misallocated?
------------------------------------------------

What I'm really worried about is that we're misallocating
our development/testing time.   Would those hours I spent adding the
new tests have been better spent doing more functional testing,
specifying interfaces for RStan/PyStan/CmdStan, or something along
those lines?

Sorry this isn't a more concrete suggestion on how to fix our process.

Maybe we can discuss at next meeting if we run out of statistical
topics.

- Bob

On Wednesday, January 1, 2014 4:47:41 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Unit testing gives me a lot of time for reflection.
>
>
> Summary
> -----------------------------------
>
> I feel we're missing the forest for the trees in testing.
>
> Given our limited time budget, I think it would be better spent
> with more functional specification and testing and less time
> unit testing.

Somewhat related to this, I think the benefit of the current function_signatures tests is not worth the time, electricity, wear on spinning hard disks, etc. I hate these tests more than I hate pennies, which I would probably value at no more than 1/10th of a cent.

I have a local branch that adds -fsyntax-only to the $(CC) call for (most of) the function_signatures tests, meaning that what is tested is whether stanc yields a .cpp file that is syntactically correct. Relative to the current behavior, it doesn't test whether the .cpp function actually compiles at whatever level of optimization. Thus, it is true that these tests might catch a rare compiler-related bug that appears at some level of optimization, it is a horrifically inefficient way of catching such bugs. Most of the function_signatures tests call different template instantiations of the same set of functions, so the compiler is doing the same optimization passes over and over again. And most of the parser bugs we have encountered either would get caught under -fsyntax-only or are run-time things that aren't getting caught by the existing behavior.

If you do

git checkout develop
make clean-all
make CC=clang++ -j9 bin/stanc
time make CC=clang++ -j4 test/gm/compile_models > /dev/null

you spend

real    42m33.405s
user    164m32.483s
sys     1m15.659s

on these tests if you don't swap, which is why I used clang++ and -j4 (my laptop has 8GB of RAM and uses 5 to 6 in this case). If you use g++, you tend to swap more. If you use mingw, you tend to swap more. If you use a recent version of mingw, instead of the 4.6.x version that comes with Rtools, you tend to swap a lot more (which is the only reason I can think of why Rtools uses such an old version of mingw). If you use -j8 with clang++ 3.4, you still swap.

With my branch that does -fsyntax-only for most of the function_signatures tests, when doing the above you spend

real    2m24.641s
user    8m38.731s
sys     0m7.217s

and can use different compilers and more virtual cores if you want. People have stated that they haven't run test-unit locally because of swapping or they specify O=0 to avoid optimization, so we would probably catch more optimization-related bugs if we did -fsyntax-only for most of the function_signatures tests and ran test-unit more often.

Some of these tests actually execute something, so I left a few of them alone, namely

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ ls src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/*.stan
src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/assignment_double_index_lhs.stan   src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/illegal_transformed_parameters.stan
src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/assignments_double_var.stan        src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/issue109.stan
src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/assignments.stan                   src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/issue91.stan
src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/assignments_var.stan               src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/mat_assign.stan
src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/declarations.stan                  src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/print_chars.stan
src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/dims.stan                          src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/print_indexing.stan
src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/domain_fail.stan                   src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/rngs.stan
src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/illegal_generated_quantities.stan  src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/value_fail.stan
src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/illegal_transformed_data.stan

I moved the rest to a function_signatures subdirectory that gets treated differently.

Ben

messages.subject: exception catching in commands/samplers?
messages.body_plain:
Exec summary:

   I'm going to let the catch errors we're getting slide
   because I don't know how to test any of my proposed fixes without
   it sucking up all my time for the foreseeable future.

Various functions in the Boost math lib throw exceptions
of various kinds:

   http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/main_overview/error_handling.html

A summary of the exception types:

   Domain Error
   Pole Error
   Overflow Error
   Underflow Error
   Denormalisation Error
   Rounding Error
   Evaluation Error
   Indeterminate Result Error

The built-in C++ exceptions are described here:

   http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/exception/exception/

There are multiple blocks in the command and samplers that set up
a try/catch, but then catch

   (a) domain_error only,
   (b) runtime_error only, or
   (c) everything.

I don't see the motivation for catching just runtime_error;  it
derives from std::exception.  Unfortunately, C++ exceptions can
be anything (though it's considered bad form to throw anything
other than a subclass of std::exception --- we don't do it and I
doubt Boost or Eigen do it).

I think we can do one of the following:

   Option 1:  just catch anything and treat it as a rejection.

      Option 1a:  literally catch anything (i.e., catch(...))

      Option 1b:  catch instances of std::exception

   Option 2:  list out a subset of each errors in duplicate catches

Option 1b is the simplest change and has the advantage over 1a of
allowing informative error messages.

But I don't know how to easily test the change in such a way as to
meet our stringent new every-code-change-must-be-tested policy.
I'd have to dive into mocking out just about every aspect of the commands
so that we could force exceptions of all the different types to be thrown so
that all the code could be exercised by tests.   This would take me days,
if not weeks of work.

So basically, I'm blocked on this the same way I'm blocked on
doing the parser fixes.  Maybe it's my own lack of imagination in
testing, but nevertheless, it's putting me off fixing this bug
that people seem to be running into (mainly from badly specified
model, but even so, we want our code to do the right thing).

We really need to review all of the command.hpp catches.
They're set up in a nesting pattern I don't understand the
motivation for (partly because the function is 700 lines long).

I would prefer to see the code factored into functions,
but then I won't get by our testing policy without testing each function.
And they're not really easy to independently test.  This is an example of
where our testing policy has the negative side effect of encouraging
monolithic functions like the 700-line long command.

So for lack of ability to test, I think I'm just going to let this
error slide for now.  Along with the parser fixes.

Suggestions appreciated.

I know Daniel said he'd help with testing when we got blocked, but he's
fully engaged on other projects, so it's no help for these relatively
simple, but hard to test fixes.

- Bob

Bob and Ben have gone off on a tangent with this email, but I think it raises important questions so...

On Wed, Jan 1, 2014 at 4:47 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Unit testing gives me a lot of time for reflection.
>
>
> Summary
> -----------------------------------
>
> I feel we're missing the forest for the trees in testing.
>
> Given our limited time budget, I think it would be better spent
> with more functional specification and testing and less time
> unit testing.

Perhaps it goes without saying but.... +1

>
>
> Example of Unit Testing Pain
> ------------------------------------
>
> To plug the memory leak in softmax, I:
>
> 1.  first verified there was a leak writing a test and then looking
> at the process in the Activity Monitor (Mac process monitor).
>
> 2.  fixed the leak by replacing "operator new" with "memalloc_.alloc".
>
> 3.  verified there was no longer a leak using the activity monitor.
>
> Now the fun begins.
>
> 4.  I wrote e-mail to the mailing list asking how to test a memory leak.
> As of 2.1.0, there was no testing at all that we aren't leaking memory.
>
> 5.  Ben suggested a Windows-incompatible test on memory, and given I
> don't know how to do the same in Windows, I didn't look further.
>
> 6. Daniel suggested monitoring stack size, but the problem was that
> the allocation wasn't happening on the stack, just on the heap, so
> I couldn't use a simple stack size test.
>
> 7.  Instead, I wrote a new function in stack_alloc that monitors the
> amount of memory allocated to Stan through memalloc_ instance.  But
> that doesn't line up real well with memory requested through
> stack_alloc::alloc due to unused bytes at the end of blocks.
>
> 8.  Then I had to go write a test for stack_alloc::bytes_allocated.  I had initially
> wanted to track memory allocated from memalloc_, but that turns out
> to be impossible given that we don't fill blocks or keep track of where
> the memory went (nor do we need to!).
>
> 9.  Next, I went back and wrote a test for softmax that failed in the
> old version and succeeded in the new version by printing out bytes
> allocated in our current code.  The key here is that the memory should've been
> allocated on this stack, not the general C++ heap.  This test is extremely brittle
> and dependent on current data structure sizes and block size constants.  It will
> have to be refiddled if we change the constants in stack_alloc or the data structures
> in softmax.   (This is an example of the kinds of problem Michael anticipated and
> we've already run into with the command-line tests.)
>
>
> What I Should Have Done
> -------------------------------------
>
> To be properly modular, what I should've done was written a new
> feature request for the bytes_allocated function, specified it, tested
> it, then written the unit test for that.
>
> Instead, I sloppily introduced a new public function in an unrelated part of
> the memory allocation code simply to support tests.
>
> At least I put it in a different commit, making sure all of the commits
> passed all of our unit tests (a huge time sink for the computer, if not
> for me).
>
>
> Was it Worth it?
> -----------------------------------
>
> All of this testing took much much much longer than the fix itself and
> involved the attention of at least three of our developers before the
> fix and will require at least one developer's time to code review.
> I think the fix took about five minutes and the unit testing about two hours,
> including writing the new functions.
>
> The end result is very brittle, and I'm not sure it's telling us anything
> that looking at the activity monitor didn't tell me (other than that it's
> automated, but as I mentioned above, that's likely to bite us later due to
> its brittleness).

Indeed, I worry about this a lot.  Some things are worth testing and can be tested well but not everything.  While having more unit tests seems like it can only be a good thing, it potentially makes large scale changes down the line impossible or incredibly time consuming to do.

Plus, all this work on low-level unit testing hasn't caught the most important kinds of bugs because we haven't gotten around to writing more high-level tests (e.g,. checking convergence or estimates from sampling).

>
>
> Subjective Nature of When Enough is Enough
> ------------------------------------------------
>
> Another problem I see is that how much testing to do is a judgment call.
> I may trust myself and code reviewers in situations like this one that
> seem totally obvious to me.  But are they totally obvious?  It's very subjective,
> and my guess is that we're all overconfident in our fixes, exactly the
> problem that unit testing is trying to mitigate.
>
> I'm not sure any of us understand Daniel's line between
> enough and not-enough testing.  (I'm only picking out Daniel because he's
> been driving this process and we put him in charge of gatekeeping merges a
> few meetings ago.)

I know I have struggled with this as well.  I think we need to come to a better consensus as a project about what "enough testing" means.

In this case, Bob ended up writing a unit test simply because the initial implementation had a bug.  I understand the need/value for regression tests but that's different from a unit test and it's unlikely that this specific bug will ever remanifest unless someone completely rewrites the code and if that happens it will most likely break the test anyway.

I think testing needs to be prioritized based on what's most important for Stan as a project.  For instance, I would rank functionality/bugs based on their urgency in the following way:

1. Statistical correctness is most urgent.  Anything which risks invalidating the results of a sufficiently long Markov chain.  Examples include correctness of PDFs or errors in the sampler.
2. Statistical efficiency is second most urgent.  Anything which slows sampling, particularly to the extent that it may lead to a user misinterpreting convergence, therefore indirectly impacting correctness.  Examples of this include correctness of gradients, bugs in adaptation, etc.
3. Crashes, memory leaks, C++ interfaces and other bugs.  These things are clearly bad but if a user hits them, they generally know and there isn't a risk of incorrect inferences.
4. User-visible interfaces.  E.G., commands do what they're supposed to, input files are read properly, output files are in the right format, etc.

My view is that our test suite should be targeted towards 1 and 2 and, to a lesser extent, 4.  Bugs and whatnot that come out of 3 are important to be fixed, but extensive unit tests aren't needed and regression tests should only be written for subtle or hard-to-notice issues.  Issues in 4 are important from a user-friendliness perspective, but I think for Stan priority #1 must be statistical correctness and efficiency and our efforts need to be prioritized accordingly.

(On a side note, if we wanted to test issues like 3 well, we should simply run all our tests/models through valgrind/dmalloc/whatever once in a while and ensure everything comes up clean.)

>
>
> Time Misallocated?
> ------------------------------------------------
>
> What I'm really worried about is that we're misallocating
> our development/testing time.   Would those hours I spent adding the
> new tests have been better spent doing more functional testing,
> specifying interfaces for RStan/PyStan/CmdStan, or something along
> those lines?
>
> Sorry this isn't a more concrete suggestion on how to fix our process.
>
> Maybe we can discuss at next meeting if we run out of statistical
> topics.

Personally I'd rather we spend some of the effort we direct towards low-level unit tests on high-level behaviour tests.  Those things matter a lot more and, if they were done, would allow us to work with less testing and more confidence elsewhere.

Cheers,
Marcus

I'm going to have to cast a vote in favor of our push for more unit tests.

Firstly, "more functionality-less tests" is really a false option.  Without tests
bugs sneak through, causing flawed releases that require a huge amount
of developer time to investigate, fix, and then update.  Not to mention the
potential breakdown of trust from our users.  I say this from experience,
loosing entire weekends tracking down bugs.

Secondly, unit tests offer far more than explicit tests.  They also offer an
example for how objects should be instantiated and used.  In our
"deprecated comments is a greater sin than no comments" philosophy
these examples are critical to understanding how someone else's code
is supposed to work and hence how it can be integrated/extended.  It seems
like half of our debugging time is spent just trying to deduce another developer's
intentions.

Thirdly, higher-level tests are extremely limited.  They can't identify problems
beyond the tested models (and there's no way we'd be able to fully test the space
of all models) and even when a problem is identified we have no guidance in
where the problems are occurring.  Yes, a bisect might be able to identify the
offending commit but it wouldn't identify interactions between the new and old
code that induce the problems.

tl;dr Unit tests not only identify bugs they make debugging easier and the
integration of new code far less difficult.  This will not change with the addition of
higher-level integration tests or statistical tests.

On 1/2/14, 8:48 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> I'm going to have to cast a vote in favor of our push for more unit tests.
>
> Firstly, "more functionality-less tests" is really a false option.  Without tests
> bugs sneak through, causing flawed releases that require a huge amount
> of developer time to investigate, fix, and then update.  Not to mention the
> potential breakdown of trust from our users.  I say this from experience,
> loosing entire weekends tracking down bugs.

I'm particularly worried about trust.  Both in ourselves and
from our users.

The problem I see is that as we crawl up the functionality and modularity
hierarchy from individual mathematical functions defined in stan::math to
the command-line code, it gets harder and harder to unit test.  The complete
spec is less clearly defined, and testing little pieces requires extensive
mock-object frameworks.  As far as I know, we don't have any tests that the
right samplers are getting called with the right command-line args, and such
tests are complex to write if we want to do it functionally, because we have
to know how each of the samplers behaves w.r.t. some fixed input.

> Secondly, unit tests offer far more than explicit tests.  They also offer an
> example for how objects should be instantiated and used.  In our
> "deprecated comments is a greater sin than no comments" philosophy
> these examples are critical to understanding how someone else's code
> is supposed to work and hence how it can be integrated/extended.  It seems
> like half of our debugging time is spent just trying to deduce another developer's
> intentions.

If you are referring to my distaste for code comments, my preference is
for better structured code (i.e., more modular code) with reasonable naming conventions
so it's easier to follow.  For instance, I'm in command.hpp right now, and there
are Fortran-style comments in functions like this:

       //////////////////////////////////////////////////
       //                Initialize Model              //
       //////////////////////////////////////////////////

to point out that the following block of code initializes the model.  I'd far
prefer a function named initialize_model(...) that encapsulated all of that code.

Functions should be short and scannable, not 700 lines of nested loops!

The problem (there's always a problem!) is that the first line is:

       Model model(data_var_context, &std::cout);

and that variable "model" is going to be needed outside the loop.  So if that
initialization is done internal the function, you have to define a nullary
constructor for Model and pass in a reference to model to set along with
the arguments.  It can quickly get ugly.  In this case, it makes sense to
define the model outside the initialization code, but I hope the general problem's
clear enough.

Also, I believe very strongly in API comments that indicate what the inputs and
outputs of functions are and how the outputs relate to the inputs.  The unit
tests can be used as stand-ins for the API comments, but I think the right way round
is to doc the API, then test vs. the doc.    Including boundary conditions.  But
this also gets much harder as we crawl up the functionality hierarchy.

Code comments should be reserved, in my opinion, for when you do something non-idiomatic
in the language or when there's a very complex algorithm the steps of which need
to be explained.

> Thirdly, higher-level tests are extremely limited.  They can't identify problems
> beyond the tested models (and there's no way we'd be able to fully test the space
> of all models) and even when a problem is identified we have no guidance in
> where the problems are occurring.  Yes, a bisect might be able to identify the
> offending commit but it wouldn't identify interactions between the new and old
> code that induce the problems.

Agreed.  And unit tests are extremely limited in exactly the opposite way --- almost
by definition, they test only micro behavior, not macro behavior.

> tl;dr Unit tests not only identify bugs they make debugging easier and the
> integration of new code far less difficult.  This will not change with the addition of
> higher-level integration tests or statistical tests.

Agreed.  The only problem is that we don't seem to get around to writing
the higher-level tests because we're all (or at least I am) buried in the
details of unit testing.

In the end, I think it's a judgment call.  I don't think we want to be dogmatic
about demanding tests for every single function at every level of abstraction.
We just don't have the programmer-hours to make progress this way.

Then again, maybe we don't have the programmer hours not to :-)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] best use of our testing time?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] best use of our testing time?
messages.body_plain:
To be clear, I don't think we should do *less* testing.  I just think we need to balance where our time is spent because I think everyones experience recently has been that we've spent a *ton* of time working on tests relative to very little time working on either bug fixes or new features.  Perhaps part of the solution is that we need to be smarter about *how* we unit test things.  "Test smarter, not harder" to paraphrase...

Let me give an example of what I mean with finite-difference gradient testing.  Right now we have finite-difference tests sprinkled all over the place.  In all of them we re-implement the same tedious steps of computing the finite difference, computing the agrad version and then comparing for some tolerance.  We clearly need a finite difference framework such that these tests would be 3-5 lines of code, tops, instead of 20 to 30.  Moreover, we have a significant collection of models and a command-line tool which computes finite-differences of the model log prob.  it should be a relatively small amount of work to actually check these as part of our unit tests.  If you just did that, without *any* specific function tests, we'd automatically get decent gradient test coverage.

I think similar arguments could be made with how we test, e.g., distribution log prob functions.

In short, right now part of why writing tests takes so much time is that it takes a lot of time to write tests.  If we make it easier to write the tests then hopefully we'll spend less time doing it.

Cheers,
Marcus

> Let me give an example of what I mean with finite-difference gradient testing.  Right now we have finite-difference
> tests sprinkled all over the place.  In all of them we re-implement the same tedious steps of computing the finite
> difference, computing the agrad version and then comparing for some tolerance.  We clearly need a finite difference
> framework such that these tests would be 3-5 lines of code, tops, instead of 20 to 30.  Moreover, we have a significant
> collection of models and a command-line tool which computes finite-differences of the model log prob.  it should be a
> relatively small amount of work to actually check these as part of our unit tests.  If you just did that, without *any*
> specific function tests, we'd automatically get decent gradient test coverage.
>
> I think similar arguments could be made with how we test, e.g., distribution log prob functions.
>
> In short, right now part of why writing tests takes so much time is that it takes a lot of time to write tests.  If we
> make it easier to write the tests then hopefully we'll spend less time doing it.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>
>
>
>
> On Thu, Jan 2, 2014 at 9:09 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com <mailto:betan...@gmail.com>> wrote:
>
>     A few quick points:
>
>      > The problem I see is that as we crawl up the functionality and modularity
>      > hierarchy from individual mathematical functions defined in stan::math to
>      > the command-line code, it gets harder and harder to unit test.  The complete
>      > spec is less clearly defined, and testing little pieces requires extensive
>      > mock-object frameworks.  As far as I know, we don't have any tests that the
>      > right samplers are getting called with the right command-line args, and such
>      > tests are complex to write if we want to do it functionally, because we have
>      > to know how each of the samplers behaves w.r.t. some fixed input.
>
>     This will definitely be improved when we refactor everything.  Unit tests are hard
>     with poor specs, but that's a problem with the spec not unit-tests.  I'm with Dan
>     in formalizing a crappy spec to get a first round of tests and then building up from there.
>
>
>      > If you are referring to my distaste for code comments, my preference is
>      > for better structured code (i.e., more modular code) with reasonable naming conventions
>      > so it's easier to follow.  For instance, I'm in command.hpp right now, and there
>      > are Fortran-style comments in functions like this:
>      >
>      >      //////////////////////////////////////////////////
>      >      //                Initialize Model              //
>      >      //////////////////////////////////////////////////
>      >
>      > to point out that the following block of code initializes the model.
>
>     So I LOVE these comments, but only because they make the relevant part of the code
>     easy to find quickly.  People will argue that command.hpp is way to long -- yeah,
>     it probably is -- but given the length these kinds of comments are helpful.
>
>     Even trivial comments on top of functions are useful as the color syntax from any decent
>     editor will make the transition between functions pop visually.  I still find the longer Stan
>     files hard to parse.
>
>      > Also, I believe very strongly in API comments that indicate what the inputs and
>      > outputs of functions are and how the outputs relate to the inputs.  The unit
>      > tests can be used as stand-ins for the API comments, but I think the right way round
>      > is to doc the API, then test vs. the doc.    Including boundary conditions.  But
>      > this also gets much harder as we crawl up the functionality hierarchy.
>      >
>      > Agreed.  And unit tests are extremely limited in exactly the opposite way --- almost
>      > by definition, they test only micro behavior, not macro behavior.
>      >
>      > Agreed.  The only problem is that we don't seem to get around to writing
>      > the higher-level tests because we're all (or at least I am) buried in the
>      > details of unit testing.
>
>     We're in a hard place right now because we're catching up for a long time without
>     tests.  It will continue to suck as we transition, but tests will be easier as we
>     formalize specs and continue the internal refactors and eventually (sooner rather
>     than later, I my opinion) we'll be in a much better place where we can get back
>     to focusing on fun code.  It will also be easier to introduce new developers and
>     external pull requests.
>
>     These are good conversations to be having!

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] best use of our testing time?
messages.body_plain:
Not trying to say anyone is writing dumb tests!  I think maybe we've taken the "path of least resistance" in writing tests a few too many times (myself certainly included) and things like this are the result: we duplicate effort and the difficulty of writing tests remains the same.

Regarding the try/catch stuff in that pull request, this is one place where I think it's reasonable to draw a line in the sand and not test everything we can possibly think of.  In my mind this is a place where some good comments, explaining why the code is written that way, would go a long ways to ensuring that it doesn't break.  Add to that a regression test which triggers the catch and, to me, that's sufficient.

Cheers,
Marcus

On 1/4/14, 6:52 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> Ideally, we'd be able to provide an ongoing estimate

>
> Doable; add it to the list.

Well said :-)

>> The problem I see with the current estimate is that it
>> gives you time for 10 leapfrog steps, but we
>> don't know how many leapfrog steps are going to be needed.
>> At the upper limit, maybe 1000 and at the lower limit, 1.
>> So it doesn't really give you an idea of how long the
>> runs are going to be.
>
> Sure, but again the warning was never intended to be taken
> that precisely.  It's original intention was to prevent people
> from spinning of runs that would take weeks without any
> warning.

I understand that, but we need to somehow convey that intent
to the users, who are really looking for a "how long will my
model take to run" estimate.  Users have
a tendency to overinterpret everything we output as being
more precise or serious than it is.
This is the same problem we've had all along with
the rejection warnings --- they say one thing and the users
interpret them another way.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] More model-specific speed decreases from 1.3 to 2.1
messages.body_plain:
Ack!  The problem is in RStan 2.1, not in the core
Stan samplers.

For this example, RStan is about 10 times slower than
CmdStan for version 2.1.

Time for 1000 warmup, 1000 sampling iterations with seed=1234
and target acceptance of 0.8 (new default in 2.1):

CmdStan:  40 seconds  ( 26s warmup,  14s sampling)
RStan:   404 seconds  (230s warmup, 175s sampling)

We'll look into what's going on and hopefully roll out a patch
for RStan ASAP (assuming it's not something that Jeff Goldsmith
and/or I did wrong in our config, in which case, we'll roll
out some better instructions).

- Bob

P.S.  I'll follow up on stan-dev list with the model and
       data in separate files.

On 1/4/14, 4:21 PM, Jeff Goldsmith wrote:
> It doesn't seem to be the multivariate implementation, just as you and Marcus suspected. I tried a slightly altered
> model using:
>
> (beta[pcur])' ~ normal(mu_beta, beta_sig[pcur]);
>
> in place of the multivariate normal. For both 1.3 and 2.1 there was a bit of a slowdown compared to the multivariate
> approach, but the sampling in 1.3 was still around 10x faster than in 2.1.
>
> I've tried altering the target acceptance rate using the argument
>
>                   control = list(adapt_delta = .65)
>
> in R. I'm not sure if this is the correct syntax, but it is what I've been using throughout and shows up in the original
> script I posted. If someone with more experience has a suggestion here, it would be very much appreciated.
>
> Thanks for the word of warning about potential biases with lower acceptance rates. In the example posted, the results in
> 1.3 and 2.1 are indistinguishable; in more systematic simulations using 1.3, there hasn't been any appreciable bias
> across many simulated datasets. The only noticeable difference is in the computation time.
>
> Best,
>
> Jeff
>
>
> On Friday, January 3, 2014 8:17:05 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>     There was a bit of slowdown in the underlying code in the
>     move from 1.3 to a more general framework in 2.0.   That
>     should be a pretty constant slowdown of less than a factor
>     of 1.5.
>
>     Then there was a big slowdown (we measured a factor of 1.5 to 2 times
>     on the BUGS models) in the move in 2.1 of a target acceptance rate of
>     0.8 from 0.65.   The upside is a reduction in bias in mean estimates
>     and better variance estimates for hierarchical models (and other models
>     with varying posterior scales).
>
>     Given that it's not the multivariate implementation, I'd suggest
>     going back to a target acceptance rate of 0.65.  The command-line option
>     is "adapt delta=0.65" to do that.  If you're using RStan, I don't know
>     what it is.
>
>     ***BUT***, as Michael keeps stressing, you need to make sure this doesn't bias your
>     results.  Do the 1.3 and 2.1 version get the same posterior means, std deviation
>     and 90% intervals?  If so, you should be OK with a reduced target acceptance rate.
>
>     - Bob
>
>     On 1/4/14, 1:22 AM, Jeff Goldsmith wrote:
>      > Thanks for the quick response, guys.
>      >

>      > Also, thanks for the tip regarding removing the uniform priors -- I know the specification is redundant, but
>     liked to
>      > keep it there to remind myself exactly what is going on. I'll take it out and see if there's a noticeable
>     difference in
>      > speed.

>      > With respect to where the change in speed is coming from (multivariate normal code or changes in the sampler
>     code), I
>      > guess I'll hold out hope that bug fixes in 2.2.0 can at least help speed things up. As I mentioned, this is a pretty
>      > simplified version of the model to illustrate the issues -- in more realistic scenarios the computation time has
>     gone
>      > from a few minutes to at least many hours.
>      >
>      > Thanks again for your input, and for all the effort done by the Stan development team on this really impressive
>     project.

>      >     acceptance rate, etc.

>      >     pretty small.

>      >
>      >             Hi all,
>      >
>      >             First, I want to express my appreciation for all the work that has gone into developing Stan -- it is
>     remarkably
>      >             user-friendly and flexible, and has a great community.
>      >
>      >             This post is similar in nature to that of Avi Feller on 12/30/13, but I thought it wouldn't hurt to
>     start a
>      >             new thread.
>      >             I've been working on problems in function-on-scalar regression -- basically, subject-level responses
>     are smooth
>      >             functions observed on a dense grid, predictors are scalars, and coefficients are smooth functions.
>      >             Coefficient functions
>      >             are estimated using a B-spline basis, so estimation and inference focuses on the B-spline
>     coefficients. I'm
>      >             attaching an

>     the spline
>      >             coefficients. This is a pretty simplified version of the model in Goldsmith & Kitago "Assessing

>      >             Effects of

>     and 2.1 are
>      >             difficult (I'm running on two different machines to keep from having to repeatedly reinstall different
>      >             versions), but my
>      >             best guess is that for the same effective sample sizes 2.1 is taking between 10 and 20 times longer than
>      >             1.3. Moreover,
>      >             the difference seems to get worse as the number of iterations increases. For more complex models, the
>      >             difference can be
>      >             much more substantial.
>      >
>      >             Any thoughts about how to speed up the code in general would be appreciated, but in particular I'm
>     wondering
>      >             if there is

>      >
>      >             Thanks for any insights the group can provide, and happy new year!

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Jeff.  You helped me realize I also had RStan 2.1
installed improperly.  I carefully RTFM this time.  No idea
what I did wrong the first time.

In fact, RStan 2.1 with g++ -O3 is a bit faster than CmdStan
with clang++ -O3:

   RStan properly installed:  33s
   CmdStan:                   40s

Maybe we need to do better buffering for CmdStan --- our output
uses std::endl, which flushes every line --- we should try replacing
it with "\n" --- we probably don't want the output to be platform-dependent
anyway.

- Bob

On 1/4/14, 8:12 PM, Jeff Goldsmith wrote:
> Thanks for the suggestions to improve speed in the model by constraining the range of support for some of the parameters
> and to run more chains in parallel. I think that will be broadly useful across a lot of models.
>
> Since I was running comparisons on two systems and getting very different results, I found a third machine to try things
> out on. This was a clean install of Stan 2.1 (rather than upgrading from 1.3 to 2.1), and most of the issues have gone
> away -- computation times are now different by the modest 50% or so that was expected all along. My guess is that in
> upgrading from 1.3 to 2.1 I did something wrong enough to slow things down immensely but not so wrong that it completely
> broke everything. My apologies for not checking this more carefully before posting, and thank you for all the input
> along the way.
>
> Best,
>
> Jeff
>
>
> On Saturday, January 4, 2014 11:34:50 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>     Looking more closely at your model, one issue
>     is that you need to constrain the parameters to their
>     support.
>
>     You have:
>
>     parameters {
>              matrix[p,Kt] beta;                     // matrix of fixed effect spline coefficients
>              real<lower=0> y_sig;             // regression variance
>              vector<lower=0>[p] beta_sig;     // tuning parameter
>     }
>
>     and then in the model:
>
>              y_sig ~ uniform(0,50);
>
>              // Prior for variance components controlling smoothness in beta
>              for(pcur in 1:p) {
>                      beta_sig[pcur] ~ uniform(0,50);
>              }
>
>     You need to add upper=50 to the declaration for y_sig and beta_sig, as in:
>
>          real<lower=0,upper=50> y_sig;
>
>     Do you expect the posterior to range over this whole range of 0 to 50?  If
>     not, tightening the interval should help sampling speed.
>
>     Your call to stan looks like this:
>
>     PFSR.fit = stan(model_name="PFSR", model_code = pfsrcode,
>                        data=dat, iter = 10000, warmup = 4000,
>                        control = list(adapt_delta = .65),
>                        chains = 1, verbose = FALSE)
>
>     I'd recommend more chains of fewer iterations, which can be run in parallel.
>
>     How long does it take the model to converge?  And how many effective samples
>     do you need?
>
>     The issue we're going to have with debugging is that the person who
>     undertands the samplers the best doesn't run R.  I'm running the models
>     now to see if I can see what's going on.

>
>     - Bob
>
>
>
>     On 1/3/14, 11:41 PM, Jeff Goldsmith wrote:
>      > The issue that I'm running into is related to computation time. Direct comparisons between Stan 1.3 and 2.1 are
>      > difficult (I'm running on two different machines to keep from having to repeatedly reinstall different versions),
>     but my
>      > best guess is that for the same effective sample sizes 2.1 is taking between 10 and 20 times longer than 1.3.
>     Moreover,
>      > the difference seems to get worse as the number of iterations increases. For more complex models, the difference
>     can be
>      > much more substantial.

I assume that it means that gamma model is much better with regards to predictive capability.  My question is why waic for the poisson model is Inf.  Data is under-dispersed and therefore I know that the poisson model is not suited well.

The simplest approach would be to just put a function waic() in rstan that looks in the output for the variable "log_lik" and, if such a variable exists, calculates Waic. messages.subject: Re: precompiling Stan as object code
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, December 1, 2013 10:07:52 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> [back on stan-dev]
>
> On 12/1/13, 5:35 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
> >> The only thing I was thinking about doing was using
> >> template instantiations as we do for the grammars
> >> so these become one-time speed costs at the expense of
> >> using much more memory.  This is just the template lib
> >> version of breaking a lib into .cpp and .hpp file.
> >
> > Is it not possible to do the same thing with the rest of Stan the library? Like instantiate one dynamically resizeable
> > Cholesky object with our scalar types?
>
> It's pretty straightforward.  Especially for Cholesky,
> which only has two instantiations until we add RHMC,
> namely Matrix<double> and Matrix<var>.
>
> The problem is that we have a lot of functions and many of
> them are far more polymorphic than the Cholesky decomposition.
>
> The worst case is for now is the Student-t density function,
> which has four arguments,  each of which can be instantiated by
>
>     double, var,
>     vector<double>, vector<var>,
>     row-vector<double>, row-vector<var>,
>     vector<var>, vector<double>, for a total of 8^4 (4096) instantiations.
>
> I don't think that will be feasible in terms of compilation time
> or object code size.
>
> With the header-based approach we take now, only the instances that
> are used in a particular model get instantiated and compiled, though
> it has to be done on a model-per-model basis.

I see what you are saying about instantiating the density functions, but can we do something about instantiating the classes we use? I have been reading about the "extern template" syntax, which is now part of the c++11 standard but has been a gcc-ism since version 3.3, so it should work with the llvm-g++-4.2 on Macs and the mingw-4.6 on Windows. This basically does explicit instantiation once and then blocks implicit instantiation in the files that use those classes.

There is a recipe for it here

http://books.google.com/books?id=gCn0wqT4W14C&lpg=PT472&ots=H8T2VMlz2O&dq=c%2B%2B11%20%22extern%20template%22&pg=PT471#v=onepage&q&f=false

and a FAQ here

http://www.stroustrup.com/C++11FAQ.html#extern-templates

Ben

On 1/14/14, 11:43 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

 > Hi, my favorite parallelism project now is the divide-and-conquer EP idea,
 > but it's not quite ready to be implemented.
 >   I think before doing the stochastic EP that is my dream algorithm, I first want to get the deterministic version
 > working, and that will have to wait until our 2nd-derivatives all programmed.

Our current approach to second derivatives work for everything
but the probability functions.  So there's no reason not to start
working on projects involving higher-order auto-diff --- you'll just
have to write the log probability function out directly in the Stan
model using log, +, /, *, exp, etc.  That's not that hard for the kind
of test problems we want to use to develop max-marginal, VB, or EP.

Michael's devised a new approach to auto-diff that is like Adept's
approach for gradients, but very cleverly generalizes to higher-order
auto-diff.   First order will be competitive with or a bit faster
than what we currently do, but higher-order should be much much
faster.

The high-level interfaces through src/stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp are
not going to change, so anything that works with the current system
should work with the new one.

We need to decide whether it's worth getting our current approach
to forward-mode working for probability functions, or just hold
off until we have the new approach working.

The new approach is a lot of work as it requires
all of the special functions in the Stan manual to have all
first (gradient vector), second (Hessian matrix), and third-order (??? tensor)
derivatives worked out analytically, coded, and tested.  And we
need to optimize the memory of the basic approach so it's fast.
We can probably get away with just the gradients to start, which
will give us the functionality we currently have exposed to users for
Stan models.

- Bob

longer than updating what we have now.  My first priority there
would be building something that's as efficient as what we have now
for gradients in *both* time and memory usage --- Daniel said he'd
be OK with a 25% slowdown, which I suppose would be OK, my only fear
being that continuing to make this same decision for every general

messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  We have a new Stan postdoc position that we are looking to fill right away!  It's a unique opportunity for someone to be working on the forefront of statistical modeling, computation, and political science.  We're looking to develop Monte Carlo EP and all sorts of other cool things, in the context of a live application.

The ideal candidate would probably be a student in CS or machine learning or maybe statistics who is a strong C++ programmer and also interested in applied Bayesian modeling.  But I think computational skills will be crucial.  If you know of any students or recent graduates who would fit this description, please let me know, also please pass this around widely:
http://andrewgelman.com/2014/01/15/postdoc-involving-pathbreaking-work-mrp-stan-2014-election/

Thanks much.
See you
Andrew

---

Postdoc involving pathbreaking work in MRP, Stan, and the 2014 election!

We’re working with polling company YouGov to track public opinion, state-by-state and district-by-district, during the 2014 campaign. We’ll be using multilevel regression and poststratification, and implementing it in Stan, and developing the necessary new parts of Stan to get this running scalably and efficiently. And we’ll be making the most detailed, up-to-date election forecasts.

What you’ll be doing if you join us as a postdoc:
- You’ll be in the midst of the most advanced polling team anywhere;
- You’ll be doing cutting-edge statistical research on MRP with deep interactions;
- You’ll be doing basic research in statistical computing, developing fast and scalable deterministic and stochastic algorithms for fitting multilevel models;
- You’ll be working inside Stan, the most advanced general computational framework for Bayesian analysis.
We’re doing research, not just implementing existing methods.

What we need:
- Stats knowledge. You should know your way around Bayesian data analysis;
- Serious computing skills. You should be a skilled C++ programmer;
- Interest in the application area. You should care about public opinion, and it should be important to you that our forecasts are good. When our estimates of opinion for some group in the population don’t make sense, you should notice and be bothered by it.

We have a great team with diverse skills (computing, statistics, political science) that plays nicely together and from whom you can learn a lot. Also lots of opportunity to collaborate with researchers in many different quantitative disciplines through Columbia’s Applied Statistics Center.

The position is a 2-year postdoc, funded by Yougov and situated in the Applied Statistics Center at Columbia University.

messages.subject: RStan compilation optimization?
messages.body_plain:
Following on from the message from Andrew and the help request
from a user, I'd like to try to automate as much as possible:

   * removing -g option from compilation

   * making sure parser and code generator compile with -O0

   * making sure lib compiles with -O3

   * making sure we don't have bogus architecture flags (e.g., -core2 for
     non core2 machines)

   * making sure models are compiled with -O3

I'm afraid if we don't, Stan installations are going to be slow and
thus hurt the user experience and tarnish our reputation.

I found the R.home() function [oddly called Rhome in the doc], but
on my machine it returns:

   > R.home()
   [1] "/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources"

rather than "~/.R/.  Digging deeper, I saw this on the FAQ:

   http://cran.r-project.org/doc/FAQ/R-FAQ.html

   Starting with R 2.1.0, users can provide personal Makevars configuration
   files in $HOME/.R to override the default flags.

Is it an OK practice to just change all the Makevars files without changing
them back?  If so, can we just automatically do that from the get go
by doing what Andrew suggests and just writing the files out.

- Bob

Mostly reasons why we need binary installs. But in the meantime, I think we just need to have the installation directions say to do

Sys.setenv(R_MAKEVARS_USER = "foobar")
options(repos = c(getOption("repos"), rstan = "http://wiki.rstan-repo.googlecode.com/git/"))
install.packages('rstan', type = 'source')
Sys.unsetenv("R_MAKEVARS_USER")

so that it will read the non-existent configuration file foobar instead of whatever the hell the user has when installing. Then,

library(rstan)
set_cppo("fast") # or set_cppo("debug")

should achieve the appropriate behavior for Stan models.

It is already frowned upon for an R package to be messing with the Makevars file. We are probably breaking a few packages that work at -O2 but not at -O3. But just take a bodyguard with you to conferences and we should be all right.

Ben

releases.  We need to balance that with fixing major problems like
leaks in softmax ASAP.

RStan other than rebuilding.

There are still a couple of issues tagged for 2.1.1, as well as some
doc updates, so I don't think we're quite there yet.  But they're all
just bug fixes, not new features.

messages.subject: new auto-diff + improved existing forward-mode
messages.body_plain:
I've been putting some cycles into evaluating Michael's new
proposal for auto-diff (I don't think they're written up anywhere ---
he just went over them one afternoon at MCMski with me and Daniel).

The basic idea is that each function stores its first, second, and
third-order derivatives, and then all of the derivatives are calculated
by multiple sweeps back and forth on the expression stack, with no
need for any further virtual function calls.

I'm still worried about the amount of memory this will take for
storing the derivatives for high-dimensional operations like dot products.
The dot product derivatives are quite structured, given that the operation
is just SUM_i x[i] * y[i].  If N is large, we wind up with an N x N
matrix of Hessians, which if you ordered the input vector x[1], y[1],
x[2], y[2], ... should just a narrow off-diagonal band.

We can probably deal with this case by de-vectorizing.  That is,
implementing dot(x,y) literally as the sum of individual products.
The downside to this is that it increases the number of items on
the stack for all the intermediate sums and products compared to what
we do now.

The other issue I worry about with the new scheme is that addition
will be less efficient because it's going to require storing the
partials where we often don't need to do that now.  This is particularly
worrisome for addition, which doesn't currently require storing the
derivatives (all 1) or multiplying them (1 * x) during derivative
propagation.

On the second topic, I just realized our forward-mode auto-diff
is horrendously inefficient for the uses we have in mind.  When
I designed it, I just naively followed existing implementations,
which defined a fwd-mode auto-diff variable as:

    template <typename T>
    fvar {
      T val_;
      T d_;
    }

(I should've used "tangent_" instead of "d_" to follow conventional
notation.)

BUT, what I now realize is that we can always take the value to
be double.  We only ever need the tangent to be an auto-diff variable.
What I should've done was this:

   template <typename T>
   fvar {
     double value_;
     T tangent_;
   }

The types are all sound because values are only ever computed in
terms of other values, whereas tangent values involve other tangents
and other values, and it's kosher to mix double and anything.

This should lead to *more* than a factor of 2 speedup because of
all the mixed operations currently done on values and tangents.
For example:

   template <typename T>
   fvar<T> multiply(const fvar<T>& x1,
                    const fvar<T>& x2) {
      return fvar<T>(x1.value_ * x2.value_,
                     x1.tangent_ * x2.value_ + x1.value_ * x2.tangent_);
   }

Here the constructor is just the obvious setter.

Current scheme:  3 multiply(var,var)
                  1 add(var,var)

New scheme:      1 multiply(double,double)
                  2 multiply(double,var)
                  1 add(var,var)

The multiply(double,double) is much faster than multiply(var,var)
and also requires substantially less memory on the stack.
The multiply(double,var) calls require the same amount of memory,
but are faster in that they eliminate a pair of multiplications
during derivative propagation.

This will result in a big savings in both memory and time
compared to the current approach.

And the savings are even more stark at third order, i.e.,
fvar<fvar<var>>, which is now just two doubles and
a var, rather than four var instances!

I actually don't think this will be a very complicated fix to
the code.  Of course, testing's going to be a pain for second
order (i.e., fvar<var>) because now the values don't need to
be pulled out of a var, they'll just be doubles.

For evaluation, I'd like to implement the new scheme far enough
that we can compare it to Michael's new scheme.  My intuition is
that our current scheme will be more memory efficient and
Michael's new scheme will be faster, even for gradients.

- Bob

> x[2], y[2], ... should just a narrow off-diagonal band.
>
> We can probably deal with this case by de-vectorizing.  That is,
> implementing dot(x,y) literally as the sum of individual products.
> The downside to this is that it increases the number of items on
> the stack for all the intermediate sums and products compared to what
> we do now.

But those items are much, much cheaper and if we’re careful about the
memory they should be as quick to access as the full Hessian in a single
joint node.  Given the new approach is should be much more efficient
to encode structure in the expression graph itself rather than internally
to a node.

> The other issue I worry about with the new scheme is that addition
> will be less efficient because it's going to require storing the
> partials where we often don't need to do that now.  This is particularly
> worrisome for addition, which doesn't currently require storing the
> derivatives (all 1) or multiplying them (1 * x) during derivative
> propagation.

We can explicitly check for 1’s in the propagation methods, although
I’d be surprised if there were a huge effect (right now we already check
for zeros to avoid unnecessary calculations).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new auto-diff + improved existing forward-mode
messages.body_plain:
Without having seen Michael's plans, it's hard to comment much on this.  However, based on Bob's description I have two thoughts:
- Is it really worth this much work to get rid of the virtual function calls?  I've really not seen them popping up in the profiles that much.  A bigger issue is making it easier to implement all the needed derivatives which this would help somewhat however, would it not be better to require each function to provide "dot_grad", "mult_hess" and "apply_3rd" (or something) and then apply those as needed?  This would allow for selective optimization of things like dot_product and sum and allow each function to make the decision of how much needs to be stored.
- I imagine we would want to template out the var type so that, if only first order derivatives are needed, no extra storage or computation is needed using, for instance, the boost::enable_if.

More broadly, I'd be interested in how this would impact functions which take matrices or vectors as parameters.  Right now our ability to implement specialized vari's for handling matrix inverses, log determinants, etc is huge for efficient computation.

Cheers,
Marcus

Participating would be a great idea.

> Probably need to focus on projects that do not actually involve much statistics.

I think it's good to provide a mix.  Some of these projects get senior undergrads and graduate students as participants so it's not strictly required that they be non-statistical.  Regardless, they should be concrete projects with limited scope.  Here are a couple of ideas:

- More flexible initialization by adding an "initialization" model block
- Optimized implementations of more distributions, e.g., make Geo BUGS models easier/faster in Stan
- Vectorization of multivariate distributions
- Implement L-BFGS and start unit testing optimization
- Parallelization

There are certainly more possibilities.  We should make a page on the wiki to keep track of ideas.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Bob:

1.  I suspect this will work for windows and linux users too, assuming the file always has that name.  To put it another way, I'd guess that if these new instructions _don't_ work with someone's install, then the existing instructions (which specify to find this file in that certain place) won't work either.  So if there might be a problem, in any case we would need a sentence in the instructions saying something like:  If these instructions don't work, you'll have to search for Makevars, which for some reason might not be in the usual place ~/.R/Makevars

I think Jiqiang or Ben will have to answer whether this could ever occur.
My guess is that R has some direct way of accessing the location of its Makevars file (e.g., a function called getMakevars()) or something like that.  This would seem to me to be more robust than hard-coding "~/.R/Makevars".  But, again, the current instructions hard-code it already, so I can't see my new instructions causing problems that weren't already there.

2.  In answer to your second question, we can just send them this R code:

if (!file.exists ("~/.R/Makevars")) cat ('CXX=g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++\nCXXFLAGS="-mtune=native  -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion"\n', file="~/.R/Makevars")

Of course, that just raises the question of why not put this R code on the website in the first place?  Or, maybe better still, 2 lines of R code, where the first line searches for the Makevars file and, if it exists, saves it with some name such as Makevars_old_current_date, and the second line is what I have above.  Then we add a note in the website saying that, if there was anything important in the old Makevars file, you can find it at ~/.R/Makevars_old_current_date

This will satisfy the needs of Andrew-syle users while also following a no-destroy policy and making everything accessible to the sophisticates.

All this of course will be superseded by our eventual one-click install…

On Wednesday, January 15, 2014 4:20:22 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Following on from the message from Andrew and the help request
> from a user, I'd like to try to automate as much as possible:
>
>    * removing -g option from compilation
>
>    * making sure parser and code generator compile with -O0
>
>    * making sure lib compiles with -O3
>
>    * making sure we don't have bogus architecture flags (e.g., -core2 for
>      non core2 machines)
>
>    * making sure models are compiled with -O3
>
> I'm afraid if we don't, Stan installations are going to be slow and
> thus hurt the user experience and tarnish our reputation.

Mostly reasons why we need binary installs. But in the meantime, I think we just need to have the installation directions say to do

Sys.setenv(R_MAKEVARS_USER = "foobar")
options(repos = c(getOption("repos"), rstan = "http://wiki.rstan-repo.googlecode.com/git/"))
install.packages('rstan', type = 'source')
Sys.unsetenv("R_MAKEVARS_USER")

so that it will read the non-existent configuration file foobar instead of whatever the hell the user has when installing. Then,

library(rstan)
set_cppo("fast") # or set_cppo("debug")

should achieve the appropriate behavior for Stan models.

It is already frowned upon for an R package to be messing with the Makevars file. We are probably breaking a few packages that work at -O2 but not at -O3. But just take a bodyguard with you to conferences and we should be all right.

Ben

> On Tue, Jan 14, 2014 at 8:46 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > Where would we put the "extern template" declaration?  And what compilation
> > would it suppress?
>
> I'm curious about this also. What would "extern template" buy us in terms of saving compilation time?

My understanding is that we have things like

Eigen::Matrix<var,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>

all over the place and the compiler has to generate a lot of code every time one of those functions gets invoked. So, the extern template mechanism outlined in the Boost recipes book tries to make it such that you can tell the compiler to generate all the necessary code for that type once in a file that gets #included by files that need it.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, November 13, 2013 9:36:45 AM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Now that it is finally officially released (to developers), I think Stan should pursue PNaCL
>
> http://blog.chromium.org/2013/11/portable-native-client-pinnacle-of.html
>
> In short, this is a Google effort that lets you use a LLVM-based compiler to create the intermediate representation of binary-ish code and then Chrome the webbrowser can execute it (in a sandbox) on the major platforms without the end-user having to compile anything or losing much speed. There is also an API for accessing local data files.

Daniel,

I have a branch that almost has this working. I have this in make/os_linux

ifeq (nacl,$(CC_TYPE))
  CFLAGS += -DBOOST_DATE_TIME_HAS_HIGH_PRECISION_CLOCK=1 -DBOOST_HAS_GETTIMEOFDAY=1
  EXE = .pexe
endif

But that just gets it to compile to the intermediate representation. So, test-unit will compile everything but not be able to execute anything.

To use or test the result, there are two more steps outlined here

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/native-client-discuss/jorIid52Se0/Gc-LsKot8RsJ

So basically, we need to makefile to notice that whenever there is a .pexe file, to do the two more steps. I put this into the makefile

##
# Tell make how to compile a .pexe file.
##
% : %.pexe
        $(patsubst %clang++,%finalize,$(CC)) -o $< $<
        $(patsubst %clang++,%translate,$(CC)) -arch linux-x86-32 -o $< $<

but that rule seems to never run.

Ben

Yeah -- I've had to deal with this a lot. In makefiles, you can't use the pattern rules with a match-all pattern on the left (%). You need to make it a static pattern rule by specifying which targets need this rule. For example
   test/foo/bar : % : %.pexe

I'm not sure if the targets are specified correctly, though. I'll have to go give it a closer look. Can you write up what you're intending it to do and what you've done so I don't have to dig too deeply? It looks like you're trying to use the EXE variable when you probably shouldn't. That was created for cross-platform compatibility. For Windows, the build targets look like Mac/Linux targets, but with a .exe at the end.

> > But that just gets it to compile to the intermediate representation. So, test-unit will compile everything but not be able to execute anything.
> >
> > To use or test the result, there are two more steps outlined here
> >
> > https://groups.google.com/d/msg/native-client-discuss/jorIid52Se0/Gc-LsKot8RsJ
> >
> > So basically, we need to makefile to notice that whenever there is a .pexe file, to do the two more steps. I put this into the makefile
> >
> > ##
> > # Tell make how to compile a .pexe file.
> > ##
> > % : %.pexe
> >         $(patsubst %clang++,%finalize,$(CC)) -o $< $<
> >         $(patsubst %clang++,%translate,$(CC)) -arch linux-x86-32 -o $< $<
> >
> > but that rule seems to never run.
>
>
> Yeah -- I've had to deal with this a lot. In makefiles, you can't use the pattern rules with a match-all pattern on the left (%). You need to make it a static pattern rule by specifying which targets need this rule. For example
>    test/foo/bar : % : %.pexe
>
> I'm not sure if the targets are specified correctly, though. I'll have to go give it a closer look. Can you write up what you're intending it to do and what you've done so I don't have to dig too deeply? It looks like you're trying to use the EXE variable when you probably shouldn't. That was created for cross-platform compatibility. For Windows, the build targets look like Mac/Linux targets, but with a .exe at the end.

OK, but it is essentially all targets that need a rule. The main goal at this point is to be able to run test-all with the pnacl compiler. Then we could propose an interface as a GSOC project, which I think would be the most attractive thing in Google's eyes because they are trying to push pnacl and lots of undergrads know HTML.

To reiterate,
pnacl-clang++ outputs an intermediate representation of the code
pnacl-finalize takes the intermediate representation and creates a platform-independent representation
Chrome the webbrowser can execute that on all platforms
but that is impossible to automatically test because you have to launch Chrome and we don't have the necessary HTML written yet. Instead,

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/native-client-discuss/jorIid52Se0/Gc-LsKot8RsJ

says that we can use pnacl-translate to take the output of pnacl-finalize and make it into an executable that runs (on 32 bit Linux for now).

So, there are two additional steps to undertake basically everywhere

$(patsubst %clang++,%finalize,$(CC)) -o $< $<
$(patsubst %clang++,%translate,$(CC)) -arch linux-x86-32 -o $< $<

but those two steps only should be run when $(CC_TYPE) is pnacl.

Maybe the thing to do is add those two lines after everywhere that $(LINK.c) is called but condition them on $(CC_TYPE) ?

Ben

As Ben pointed out, it may break other packages that won't compile

said we should bring bodyguards to conferences :-)

So, I did as you asked and added this to the instructions:

   One way you can achieve this is to execute this from within R:

   if (!file.exists("~/.R/Makevars")) {

On 1/19/14, 8:53 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> Without having seen Michael's plans, it's hard to comment much on this.

I'd write it up, but it's pretty complicated and I still only
understand it up to second order.  (Though Michael says 3rd order
is just more of the same and he has it working for a few operations.)

 > However, based on Bob's description I have two
> thoughts:
> - Is it really worth this much work to get rid of the virtual function calls?
 > I've really not seen them popping up in
 > the profiles that much.

Absolutely.  Check out the Adept paper, which is the
first-order version of what Michael's doing:

http://www.met.reading.ac.uk/clouds/adept/

The real benefit, though, is at higher orders, because
nothing needs to get recalculated other than a string
of multiply-adds.  As we're doing things now, we run
the whole log prob function on an fvar<var> for each parameter
to compute a row of the Hessian.  But all the partials, which
is where the real work is with all the exps, gamma functions
and what not, get recomputed each time.

> A bigger issue is making it easier to implement all the needed derivatives which this would
> help somewhat however, would it not be better to require each function to provide "dot_grad", "mult_hess" and
> "apply_3rd" (or something) and then apply those as needed?  This would allow for selective optimization of things like
> dot_product and sum and allow each function to make the decision of how much needs to be stored.

Yes, we absolutely need to do that so that we can still
run Euclidean HMC quickly.  All we need per function is
the local gradient vector, Hessian matrix, and tensor
of 3rd order derivatives.

> - I imagine we would want to template out the var type so that, if only first order derivatives are needed, no extra
> storage or computation is needed using, for instance, the boost::enable_if.

Right.

> More broadly, I'd be interested in how this would impact functions which take matrices or vectors as parameters.  Right
> now our ability to implement specialized vari's for handling matrix inverses, log determinants, etc is huge for
> efficient computation.

This is my main concern, too.  The problem with having to do
Hessians for something like a dot product is that they're mostly
zeroes.  The alternative is unfolding it into a sequence of products
and sums, which defeats the speed of what we have in there now.

And doing something like matrix inverse is even worse as far as this
goes.  Without solutions to these problems, I think the new
approach is a non-starter.

Having said all this, I have a scheme to make the existing forward-mode
much faster.

- Bob

> Cheers,
> Marcus
>
>
>
> On Sun, Jan 19, 2014 at 2:02 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com <mailto:betan...@gmail.com>> wrote:

>
>
>     On Jan 19, 2014, at 1:39 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>
>      > I've been putting some cycles into evaluating Michael's new
>      > proposal for auto-diff (I don't think they're written up anywhere ---
>      > he just went over them one afternoon at MCMski with me and Daniel).
>      >
>      > The basic idea is that each function stores its first, second, and
>      > third-order derivatives, and then all of the derivatives are calculated
>      > by multiple sweeps back and forth on the expression stack, with no
>      > need for any further virtual function calls.
>      >
>      > I'm still worried about the amount of memory this will take for
>      > storing the derivatives for high-dimensional operations like dot products.
>      > The dot product derivatives are quite structured, given that the operation
>      > is just SUM_i x[i] * y[i].  If N is large, we wind up with an N x N
>      > matrix of Hessians, which if you ordered the input vector x[1], y[1],
>      > x[2], y[2], ... should just a narrow off-diagonal band.
>      >
>      > We can probably deal with this case by de-vectorizing.  That is,
>      > implementing dot(x,y) literally as the sum of individual products.
>      > The downside to this is that it increases the number of items on
>      > the stack for all the intermediate sums and products compared to what
>      > we do now.
>

>     But those items are much, much cheaper and if weï¿½re careful about the

>     memory they should be as quick to access as the full Hessian in a single
>     joint node.  Given the new approach is should be much more efficient
>     to encode structure in the expression graph itself rather than internally
>     to a node.
>
>      > The other issue I worry about with the new scheme is that addition
>      > will be less efficient because it's going to require storing the
>      > partials where we often don't need to do that now.  This is particularly
>      > worrisome for addition, which doesn't currently require storing the
>      > derivatives (all 1) or multiplying them (1 * x) during derivative
>      > propagation.
>

>     We can explicitly check for 1ï¿½s in the propagation methods, although
>     Iï¿½d be surprised if there were a huge effect (right now we already check

>     for zeros to avoid unnecessary calculations).

> So you're proposing to break something like dot product
> apart into a series of multiply-adds?  It will take quite
> a bit more memory that way, and I don't see how it'd work
> with something like matrix operations like division (or
> inverse or determinant or whatever).

For the dot product, yes.  Dense matrix operations will have dense
derivatives and be different beasts.

Splitting things up should only introduce a few extra ints/bools for indexing
and defining order.  To get rid of that we'd need some container class or something
and I'm not sure how to do that without bringing in virtual functions.

> I don't know this for sure, but my guess would be that checking
> for 1 would be as expensive as multiplying by 1.  Branching is
> expensive!

Let’s be clear — the new approach admits very fast matrix computations
by efficiently computing all of the partials in the instantiation of a node
(leveraging Eigen to its full effect).

The issue here is when we define an operation that has sparse or structure
(but non-zero) higher-order derivatives.  Currently we would not take
advantage of this structure and perform unnecessary loops/operations.
Splitting out the nodes would encode the structure in the expression
graph itself, allowing a compromise between the two approaches.

> zeroes.  The alternative is unfolding it into a sequence of products

> goes.  Without solutions to these problems, I think the new
> approach is a non-starter.

> Having said all this, I have a scheme to make the existing forward-mode
> much faster.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new auto-diff + improved existing forward-mode
messages.body_plain:
On 1/20/14, 3:13 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Letï¿½s be clear ï¿½ the new approach admits very fast matrix computations

> by efficiently computing all of the partials in the instantiation of a node
> (leveraging Eigen to its full effect).

That's what we do now, with the added overhead of
copying the values of the var into a new matrix.

I don't understand your proposal (both my calc and matrix algebra
fu are weak).  If you have an N x N matrix and take an inverse,
what's the Hessian and how do you encode it (if necessary)?

> The issue here is when we define an operation that has sparse or structure
> (but non-zero) higher-order derivatives.  Currently we would not take
> advantage of this structure and perform unnecessary loops/operations.

A dot product like

   z = SUM_i x[i] * y[i]

has a sparse local Hessian, with only d^2/dx[i]dy[i] = 1 and all other
entries zero.

> Splitting out the nodes would encode the structure in the expression
> graph itself, allowing a compromise between the two approaches.

I think we're talking about the same thing here --- define a bunch of
intermediate x[i] * y[i] nodes, each of which has the same (2 x 2) Hessian
(with 0 diagonal and 1 off diagonal entries).

And then a single node for the sum (only a gradient, no higher-order
derivatives);  you could also use N binary sums.

I think I see what the booleans are doing now --- that's for when
the Hessian's all zero?  That comparison's not free, but definitely
better than the alternative!

Either way, the new approach will take much more memory than what we do now and
require more multiplies by 1 (we can skip that because the dot-product knows that
the gradient is 1).

Right now, for computing gradients, the dot product of two var N-vectors consumes
a total of 2N+2 pointers + 1 size_t (the 2N for the daughters, one for the mother, and one
for the vtable pointer; size_t is for the size).  Plus there's one more pointer on the
actual stack to the memory used.  The product of a double and var takes the same amount
of memory, but has fewer propagation ops --- presumably that would be the same in
what you're doing.

With the new scheme I was proposing for reducing
memory in fvar, the Hessian calc won't take much more memory per pass, but
there's the inevitable (2N)^2 entries in the final Hessian.  This is assuming
I'm remembering correctly that you need an explicit Hessian for SoftAbs
and not just a Hessian-vector product.

- Bob
