messages.body_plain:
There are two parts to the Adept auto-diff system.

One's the templating, and yes, that'd make compilation times
even worse.  I'm not convinced it's worth the coding hassle
given how many functions we have to deal with.

The other is that it just creates an expression graph consisting
only of nodes and partials, so that the backward pass is just
a bunch of add/multiply ops.  Exactly what we're doing for
the probability functions, but without any need for the virtual
function call.

Michael figured out how to extend that scheme to higher-order
derivatives.  Actually, Michael just figured it out from
scratch --- only after he explained it did I tell him it
was like what Adept was doing.  I'd experimented with the
same scheme a while ago, but couldn't really get it to go
any faster than what we had, but I'm not sure I fully got
rid of the virtual function calls.

The downside of Adept compared to what we're doing now is
that it can be more memory intensive.  For instance, in
sums, we only have pointers to the daughter nodes, whereas
the Adept scheme has pointers (really just indexes, and they
use int for that, not actual pointers) and also the partials
for the edges.  We are lazy about computing many of the partials,
which saves memory in cases other than just sum.  For instance,
an exp node doesn't need to store a partial and a daughter,
just the daughter, because the partial's recoverable as the
value.  On the other hand, the Adept-like scheme doesn't
need to store a vtable pointer.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Ok, I see your concern with memory but I'm not sure that's much different than what we're doing now.  We already have to store the value and an adjoint for everything.  For more complex operations we end up storing a bit more than that (e.g., matrix factorizations).  Sure it will get nastier with higher order derivatives, but, to some extent, that's unavoidable.  So long as we can

1. Make the expression graph smaller by compressing things with specializations of the expression templates, and
2. Implement special traversals of the expression graph to efficiently implement things like Hessian-vector products

then it seems plausible.  I'm still not seeing at all why dot_product would have to be done in terms of scalar ops though...  Also, just to be clear, it's not really dot_product that worries me most, it's things like mdivide_left.  If we have to do dot_product with scalar ops, does that mean we have to do mdivide_left (and hence, Cholesky/QR/etc) with scalar ops?  If so that's really bad but right now I don't see why that has to be the case.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new auto-diff + improved existing forward-mode
messages.body_plain:
To review:

Forward mode computes scalars, namely,

v^{i} partial_{i} phi
v^{i} w^{j} partial_{i} partial{j} phi
v^{i} w^{j} x^{k} partial_{i} partial_{j} partial_{k} phi

efficiently, and because only one sweep is necessary memory
can be allocated on the stack and grows only as the largest node.

Reverse mode computes vectors, namely

partial_{i} phi
v^{i} partial_{i} partial_{j} phi
v^{i} w^{j} partial_{i} partial_{j} partial_{k} phi,

efficiently, at the expense of having to store everything
on the heap.  The savings are significantly, at least an order
of N faster than forward mode.

The new method computes both forward and reverse mode,
but focuses on saving the expression graph so that multiple
sweeps can be made without duplicating any partial evaluations.
It could easily be modified to do forward mode with allocation
only on the stack.

Now the expanded memory footprint for reverse mode goes as
the size of the largest node, which in most cases will be dwarfed
by the size of the full expression graph.  Higher-order partials
follow a similar pattern.  In particular, the footprint should
grow with some coefficient times the size of the problem,
and if memory is an issue then there are going to be much worse
problems with higher-order methods (RHMC NUTS uses way
more memory than this).  In particular, if we template out first-order
and higher-order executables then the memory footprint should be
manageable for really big models.

Now, that said, there are many optimizations that could be made
if we admit polymorphism.  Dynamic polymorphism is slow,
static would require a change to the modeling language (loops
are fine, the bounds just have to be constants).  Adept very
elegantly used expression templates for static polymorphism
which also allowed the compiler to compile away all kinds of
optimizations.

> an exp node doesn't need to store a partial and a daughter,

No, you can _compute_ everything with matrix ops, the results just have to stored in many-to-one nodes.
So an N-to-M function would be stored in the graph as M N-to-1 node, but we can do all of the N-to-M
linear algebra efficiently when we compute all those partials.

Instantiation (i.e. computing the partials) can be specialized right now, it’s just traversal of the graph
that has to be generalized.

If we have to do dot_product with scalar ops, does that mean we have to do mdivide_left (and hence, Cholesky/QR/etc) with scalar ops?  If so that's really bad but right now I don't see why that has to be the case.

messages.subject: sharing code in Py/R/CmdStan: effective_sample_size
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

There are many opportunities for eliminating extra implementations of identical
functionality in PyStan/RStan/CmdStan. For example, there are three
implementations of effective_sample_size (and split_potential_scale_reduction).

I'd like to get that number down to two by eliminating the version in PyStan
and just using the functions in stan/mcmc/chains.hpp from Python.

Python's Rcpp, called Cython, handles C++ vectors without any trouble. So the
main challenge is just what to do about moving between a C++ vector and an Eigen
VectorXd. As this seems like it might be a general concern, I thought I'd raise
the question of an appropriate strategy on the list.

One thought I had is that in the areas where a simple conversion is required,
Stan might expose a function that accepts a vector in addition to a version
that accepts a VectorXd.

Thanks,

-a

An alternative to converting to std::vector<> would be to use minieigen[1], pyeigen[2], or similar Eigen bindings for Python, which provide similar functionality to RcppEigen[3], which provides R bindings for Eigen.  (These are broader than just VectorXd, and may not require a copy to an STL vector, which could save time for large vectors.)

Last I checked, the two Python bindings I mentioned were still under development, but they may have matured by now.  Even if they haven't fully matured, the VectorXd bindings/parts are probably stable.  I've used RcppEigen and it's pretty stable.

Sorry in advance if you've already considered this and I'm just stating the obvious. :-)

Ido

[1] https://pypi.python.org/pypi/minieigen
[2] https://launchpad.net/pyeigen
[3] http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RcppEigen/index.html

This was, by the way, one of the reasons I thought
std::vector interfaces would be easier and more portable.

What Michael's suggesting is probably the path of least
resistance and shouldn't be inefficient (other than to
compile).

A more idiomatic approach within C++ would be to define the
interfaces in terms of iterators.  A more generic way to do
it with references to container arguments would be to template
out the container type and just use accessors (for example, []
works for arrays, standard vectors, C++11 arrays, Eigen vectors, and
many of the Boost sequence containers).  The cost is that the code's a
bit more complex, which is why we've (or at least I've) tended not
to do it that way.  But I think we're all getting better at C++,
so maybe this shouldn't be such a hurdle any more.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: language design for ODE solvers
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Bob.  I admit to liking things that are close to MCSim; whether that's because I'm more familiar with it or because it's better, I'm not sure.

You are creating a simulator that can work for system dynamics modeling, too.  As you ask for libraries of models, http://www.metasd.com/models/ is a collection of system dynamics models.  Some of the Vensim models are just text, so you can examine those.  Others may require the Vensim model reader from http://www.vensim.com/ or the iThink model player from http://www.iseesystems.com/, both of which are free.  Follow the direction on Tom Fiddaman's page.

A system dynamics simulator pretty much requires the ability to specify a tabular nonlinear function with some sort of interpolation between defined points.  I know Stan is not compatible with the GPL, but I use GSL Akima interpolation routines in MCSim.  I'm confident Boost has something similar.

Finally, you might be interested in XMILE (http://xmile.systemdynamics.org/ and https://www.oasis-open.org/committees/tc_home.php?wg_abbrev=xmile), the XML Interchange Language for System Dynamics.

If you're not sure what system dynamics is, see http://www.systemdynamics.org/what-is-s/.  Despite them using DE notation, too, most system dynamics models are written as integral equations, something like

state = integrate(netflow, initialconditions)

and better modeling systems allow for the use of units and units checking with suitable units algebra checking.

Bill

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] language design for ODE solvers
messages.body_plain:
I have opinions!  :-)  Oh, and for future reference it's the "simple harmonic oscillator" or "sho".  "ho" just looks weird.  :-p

I immediately don't like (3) because I think it will lead to no end of errors from scope confusing and naming conflicts.  I am a big fan of more strict syntax that prevents these kinds of collisions.

So that leaves (1) and (2).  I like the simplicity of (2)'s syntax (I'm already fearing the ridiculous signatures that would arise from user models if a fully generic (1) were implemented as is) but can see the huge restriction of limiting our users to reals.
That said, is there a way to combine them?  I'm thinking of having data, parameter, and state classes which are just polymorphic containers for Stan variables.  So when you define

differential equations {
  harmonic_oscillator {
    ...
    parameters {
      real<lower=0> gamma;
    }
    …
}

the user would have access to the new type

harmonic_oscillator::parameters

which they could use as

harmonic_oscillator::parameters::gamma <- 5;

Then we get the simple signature of (2) but the user has the freedom of defining different types while also having a clear understanding of their scope.

messages.subject: major holes in existing fwd-mode
messages.body_plain:
I realized when writing the new tests for diag_post_multiply
that it was only written for fvar * fvar, not for double * fvar
or fvar * double.  I'm guessing from this that it's a widespread
problem that was never caught in the original testing.

This means there's a lot more work to do to get the existing
forward mode working.

I can add implementations for these and then fix the tests,
but is that the right thing to do?  It's certainly the path
of least resistance for me to get by our testing requirements.
Although the truly least path would be to sneak by a test that only
tested fvar * fvar, which now works, but I like to stay honest here
and try to do what's expected of me.

One option would be to just rip out all the forward mode we
currently have in anticipation of the new one.  But I want
to have the current one around for testing.

Also, if we're going to use the current version, it should
really be updated to deal with mixed types:

   template <typename Tval=double, typename Td=Tval>
   struct fvar {
     Tval val_;
     Td d_;
   }

This would make all the second-order calculations go much faster.

- Bob

messages.subject: tangled in Git again
messages.body_plain:
OK, I ran into another Git SNAFU working on the
branch

    bugfix/issue-464-diag_pre_multiply

which branched from

   hotfix/v2.1.1

Somehow the test rug got pulled out from under my feet and
I'm going to need help getting myself out of this mess.

I've attached the new test, which is the only thing I was
trying to add at this juncture.  The good news is the
test works.  The bad news is I have no friggin' clue what
to do from here.  Here's what happened in case that helps.

I added the test locally and committed it, no problem.

~/stan(bugfix/issue-464-diag_pre_multiply)$ git commit -a -m "added and verified a thorough diag_post_multiply test"
[bugfix/issue-464-diag_pre_multiply f24c9dd] added and verified a thorough diag_post_multiply test
  1 file changed, 316 insertions(+), 823 deletions(-)
  rewrite src/test/agrad/fwd/matrix/diag_post_multiply_test.cpp (98%)

Then I tried to push, but no luck.

~/stan(bugfix/issue-464-diag_pre_multiply)$ git push
To https://github.com/stan-dev/stan.git
  ! [rejected]        bugfix/issue-464-diag_pre_multiply -> bugfix/issue-464-diag_pre_multiply (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/stan-dev/stan.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing
hint: to the same ref. You may want to first merge the remote changes (e.g.,
hint: 'git pull') before pushing again.
hint: See the 'Note about fast-forwards' in 'git push --help' for details.

So, I tried to pull hotfix/v2.1.1 from origin

~/stan(bugfix/issue-464-diag_pre_multiply)$ git pull origin hotfix/v2.1.1

and all hell broke loose.  Now I'm going to need help figuring out where
to go from here.  Below is what I got after running the above (and below that, what I
got from running "git status"

- Bob

messages.subject: suggestion for improving make help
messages.body_plain:
I should add that the new test I added somehow got moved
after the pull into

   src/test/unit-agrad-fwd/matrix/diag_post_multiply_test.cpp

I struggled to understand "make help", but there weren't any
instructions on how to run a single unit test.  Eventually
I figured out that I needed to remove the src and give the new
path to the test:

   $ mk test/unit-agrad-fwd/matrix/diag_post_multiply

and then run it on its own, because the above just makes it

   $ ./test/unit-agrad-fwd/matrix/diag_post_multiply

I'd specifically suggest replacing these instructions

  Tests (requires make 3.81 or higher):
   - test-headers   : Compiles a trivial file after including each
                      header separately
   - For any subdirectory directory in *src/test*, all tests within
     the specified directory and subdirectories can be compiled
     and executed by using the folder as the target (without a trailing slash).
     Examples:
     * all unit tests:            src/test/unit
     * unit tests for meta:       src/test/unit/meta
     * normal distribution tests: src/test/unit-distribution/univariate/continuous/normal
   - test-all       : Runs all tests.

with

  TESTS (requires make 3.81 or higher)

    All Tests
      - test-all

    Header Tests
      - test-headers

    Unit Tests
      The unit tests are broken into three targets:
        - src/test/unit
        - src/test/unit-agrad-rev
        - src/test/unit-agrad-fwd

    Subdirectory of Unit Tests
      For example, to run the unit tests under meta
        - src/test/unit/meta

    Single Unit Test
      For example, to run the diag_post_multiply test, make the target
        - test/unit-agrad-fwd/matrix/diag_post_multiply
      Then run the test outside of make by executing
        ./test/unit-agrad-fwd/matrix/diag_post_multiply

It would be nice if there was an easier way to run a single unit test directly
from make.  It's awkward having to enter two commands and I do this all the time
That is, I don't want to have to run all the matrix forward tests when I'm just
working on one of them.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] tangled in Git again
messages.body_plain:
So I didn't see the output from git status, but I'm guessing you have some conflicts?  At the very least I'm pretty certain you still won't be able to push.

Anyway, I think the issue is that you actually needed to do a:

git pull origin bugfix/issue-464-diag_pre_multiply

(or, probably equivalently just git pull)

I'm not sure the best way to fix it.  I think you need to do a:

git reset --hard YOURCOMMIT

where YOURCOMMIT is the commit with the test before you did the git pull.  Then do the git pull from the bugfix branch and you should be good to go.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] language design for ODE solvers
messages.body_plain:
I also think (3) is a bad idea.  I think those kinds of weird scoping rules just lead to unexpected surprises.  Plus, so far Stan has been pretty strict in it's language (e.g., requiring explicit declaration of variables) so (1) or (2) definitely seems more "natural" in that sense.

Personally, i'd vote for (2) for a two reasons.  First, it's a familiar style of interface for ODE solvers so I think most people will be comfortable with it.  (1) is more expressive, but is going to be tricky to get right, e.g., what happens if a user defines constrained parameters, how are initial conditions passed in when there are multiple parameters, how is the result returned?  Second, I think in the process of implementing (2) it would be easy to at least lay the groundwork for more general user-defined functions in Stan which is a feature that's been on the wish-list for a long time and would help clean-up more complex models.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Thu, Jan 30, 2014 at 7:00 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> That's similar to some ideas Andrew had, and my thought is
> that it would be best to do by adding a new list-like type
> to Stan.
>
> I'm also not keen on (3), hence my blog post on Andrew's blog
> about R's behavior.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On 1/30/14, 12:53 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> > I have opinions!  :-)  Oh, and for future reference it's the "simple harmonic oscillator" or "sho".  "ho" just looks
> > weird.  :-p
> >
> > I immediately don't like (3) because I think it will lead to no end of errors from scope confusing and naming conflicts.
> >   I am a big fan of more strict syntax that prevents these kinds of collisions.
> >
> > So that leaves (1) and (2).  I like the simplicity of (2)'s syntax (I'm already fearing the ridiculous signatures that
> > would arise from user models if a fully generic (1) were implemented as is) but can see the huge restriction of limiting
> > our users to reals.
> > That said, is there a way to combine them?  I'm thinking of having data, parameter, and state classes which are just
> > polymorphic containers for Stan variables.  So when you define
> >
> > differential equations {
> >    harmonic_oscillator {
> >      ...
> >      parameters {
> >        real<lower=0> gamma;
> >      }

> >      ...

> >
> > }
> >
> > the user would have access to the new type
> >
> > harmonic_oscillator::parameters
> >
> > which they could use as
> >
> > harmonic_oscillator::parameters::gamma <- 5;
> >
> > Then we get the simple signature of (2) but the user has the freedom of defining different types while also having a
> > clear understanding of their scope.
> >
> >
> >
> > On Wed, Jan 29, 2014 at 8:20 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
> >
> >     I updated the doc with some proposals if anyone has
> >     any comments:

> >     https://github.com/stan-dev/__stan/wiki/ODE-Integrator-__Support

> >
> >     Proposal 2 is by far the easiest to code, but I think Proposal 3 is
> >     the most natural.  I had originally thought we'd go with Proposal 1,
> >     but I also think that'll be both too tricky to code and for users to
> >     call and also too redundant.
> >
> >     - Bob

One way to ease this is to allow an arbitrary number of parameters to be passed in.  The state vector would still need to packed and unpacked but it would reduce the complexity otherwise.  For instance, you could do:

vector[] harmonic_oscillator(real t, vector[] state, real param1, vector[] param2, matrix[] param3) {
...
}

and then when calling

solutions <- ode_solve(harmonic_oscillator,
                       intial_state,
                       solution_times,
                       param1, param2, param3);

Basically, allow the function to take an arbitrary number of parameters of any type and when ode_solve is called, anything after the initial state and solutions times gets passed in to the function.

Cheers,
Marcus

Bob,

Two more thoughts.

First, you keep writing of Jacobians.  I think most system dynamicists

On 1/31/14, 7:34 AM, Bill Harris wrote:
> Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> writes:
>
>> Thanks for the thoughtful note!  I added it to our design doc
>> along with Ben's notes on definitions of densities
>> through diffeqs.  As much as I find this all a bit overwhelming,
>> it's probably better to have a heads-up now rather than later.
>

>
> Two more thoughts.
>
> First, you keep writing of Jacobians.  I think most system dynamicists
> wouldn't know what to do about writing a Jacobian of their model, but
> it's been so long since I've had to do anything practical with them that
> I'll have to do some study.

What I mean here is that we need the Jacobian of the system.
And by system here, I just mean the function that takes the state
and provides the derivatives w.r.t. time of the state at a given
point.  So if you have x[1] and x[2] as the state (inputs), then the
diff eq system defines y[1] = d/dt x[1] and y[2] = d/dt x[2] (outputs).
So the system is a function f(x) = y, and what we need is the Jacobian
of the function, namely dy / dx, which is just dy[n] / dx[m] for n in 1:2
and m in 1:2.

They're pretty standard in solving diff eqs.  For instance, both Boost
and dSolve in R require user-supplied Jacobians to solve stiff systems.

> I'm presuming that Jacobians are needed for HMC; I don't recall anything
> about Jacobians in MCSim.

No, we only need gradients of the solutions w.r.t. the parameters
for HMC.  So if that function f(x) = y depends on some parameters,
that is, f(x) = y depends on alpha and beta, then we need the
gradients of y w.r.t. alpha and beta.

> To the degree that the calculation of Jacobians can be done
> automatically, that's great.

We absolutely want to compute them automatically, so that users
will only have to specify the function f(x) = y in a way that
may involve parameters (as well as constants).

> To the degree they need to be coded, I
> suspect a significant number of your potential users may need clear
> help.
>
> Second, I recall the biggest problem I have with MCSim and, for that
> matter, to a degree with some commercial simulators: the ability to
> encapsulate submodels.
>
> For example, say I create a system dynamics (ODE) model of a supply
> chain, and I have a planning function as part of that model.  The supply
> chain is fairly clear to code and diagram, but the planning function
> complicates the picture for the reader.  isee systems' iThink used to
> have a DFD (Decision Flow Diamond) that would hide parts of models.  In
> this case, I could put the entire planning function inside a DFD and
> expand it only when I needed to see it.  Otherwise, I'd just look at the
> main supply chain and realize there was a planning function that was
> intended to take care of keeping it filled.

> In a non-graphical system such as MCSim or Stan, it might be that you
> can encapsulate dynamic bits (some of the ODEs) in a function that gets
> called by the higher-level model.

That's the plan.  Unless we get very directed funding or volunteers,
it's unlikely we're going to do anything specific for any of these
model classes.

> I'll have to look tomorrow: I presume that state variables and their
> derivatives can be non-scalar, right?  MCSim has a decent array
> functionality, as do most professional SD simulators.  That's quite
> handy when you have the same structure repeated but perhaps with
> different paramater values.

The plan for now is to have the system be arrays.  But you could
pack anything into those arrays.  This is what MCSim and Boost's
solvers do.  For instance, MCSim doesn't have any matrix or 2D
array functionality.  Part of what we're trying to think about is
how critical that'll be.  It probably won't go in our first implementation
even if we do think it's critical.  We just don't have much time to
work on this subsystem of Stan.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob,

Okay; I think I see.  Simulators I have used essentially encode the
Jacobian in a set of equations that essentially describe each element
of the Jacobian in one of the equations.  If an element isn't
described by some such equation, then the entry is de factor 0 for
that cell of the Jacobian, right?

SD modelers and perhaps others are taught to think structurally about
the problem, so that encoding is nice; a separate Jacobian matrix
definition would not be seen as a transparent model.  (Most SD models
have associated "stock and flow" or "influence diagram" graphical
representations that show how stocks / state variables and flows /
derivatives connect together, something loosely like PBPK
compartmental model diagrams

Moreover, each element of a Jacobian / definition of the inflows and
outflows to or from a stock / derivative of (net inflow to) a stock
can be a complex, tabularly-defined nonlinear function, which might be
awkward to put into a matrix.

So I think we're saying much the same thing (and writing about
Jacobians just before going to sleep as I did last night is risky;
obviously that's what a Jacobian is).  If you lead with Jacobians, I
suspect some will be scared off.

On a second topic, I don't see any need to do predefined complex
submodels up front or perhaps ever.  There is an advantage to
providing an easy-to-use, expressive language and then making people
think through what they're doing (system dynamics languages, Stan,
MCSim, and R all fit that mold)  There is a different, productivity
advantage to a language heavily supported by libraries (packages) such
as R.  Vensim does provide such a thing for Vensim models; see
http://vensim.com/modeling-with-molecules-2-02/.

Oh, and have you seen http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBML?  MCSim works
with SBML, I think, but I've never used it.

Finally, http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DYNAMO_(programming_language)
speaks to the original SD language.  Several books listed in the
bibliography describe that language, and section 3.7 of
http://eprints.cs.vt.edu/archive/00000363/01/TR-93-21.pdf shows an
example.  Even though it's over 50 years old, it still has a strong
influence on SD modeling languages.  FYI / FWIW.

Bill

On Fri, Jan 31, 2014 at 6:50 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>
> On 1/31/14, 7:34 AM, Bill Harris wrote:
>>
>> Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> writes:
>>
>>> Thanks for the thoughtful note!  I added it to our design doc
>>> along with Ben's notes on definitions of densities
>>> through diffeqs.  As much as I find this all a bit overwhelming,
>>> it's probably better to have a heads-up now rather than later.
>>
>>
>> Bob,
>>
>> Two more thoughts.
>>
>> First, you keep writing of Jacobians.  I think most system dynamicists
>> wouldn't know what to do about writing a Jacobian of their model, but
>> it's been so long since I've had to do anything practical with them that
>> I'll have to do some study.
>
>
> What I mean here is that we need the Jacobian of the system.
> And by system here, I just mean the function that takes the state
> and provides the derivatives w.r.t. time of the state at a given
> point.  So if you have x[1] and x[2] as the state (inputs), then the
> diff eq system defines y[1] = d/dt x[1] and y[2] = d/dt x[2] (outputs).
> So the system is a function f(x) = y, and what we need is the Jacobian
> of the function, namely dy / dx, which is just dy[n] / dx[m] for n in 1:2
> and m in 1:2.
>
> They're pretty standard in solving diff eqs.  For instance, both Boost
> and dSolve in R require user-supplied Jacobians to solve stiff systems.
>
>
>> I'm presuming that Jacobians are needed for HMC; I don't recall anything
>> about Jacobians in MCSim.
>
>
> No, we only need gradients of the solutions w.r.t. the parameters
> for HMC.  So if that function f(x) = y depends on some parameters,
> that is, f(x) = y depends on alpha and beta, then we need the
> gradients of y w.r.t. alpha and beta.
>
>
>> To the degree that the calculation of Jacobians can be done
>> automatically, that's great.
>
>
> We absolutely want to compute them automatically, so that users
> will only have to specify the function f(x) = y in a way that
> may involve parameters (as well as constants).
>
>
>> To the degree they need to be coded, I
>> suspect a significant number of your potential users may need clear
>> help.
>>
>> Second, I recall the biggest problem I have with MCSim and, for that
>> matter, to a degree with some commercial simulators: the ability to
>> encapsulate submodels.
>>
>> For example, say I create a system dynamics (ODE) model of a supply
>> chain, and I have a planning function as part of that model.  The supply
>> chain is fairly clear to code and diagram, but the planning function
>> complicates the picture for the reader.  isee systems' iThink used to
>> have a DFD (Decision Flow Diamond) that would hide parts of models.  In
>> this case, I could put the entire planning function inside a DFD and
>> expand it only when I needed to see it.  Otherwise, I'd just look at the
>> main supply chain and realize there was a planning function that was
>> intended to take care of keeping it filled.
>
>
>> In a non-graphical system such as MCSim or Stan, it might be that you
>> can encapsulate dynamic bits (some of the ODEs) in a function that gets
>> called by the higher-level model.
>
>
> That's the plan.  Unless we get very directed funding or volunteers,
> it's unlikely we're going to do anything specific for any of these
> model classes.
>
>
>> I'll have to look tomorrow: I presume that state variables and their
>> derivatives can be non-scalar, right?  MCSim has a decent array
>> functionality, as do most professional SD simulators.  That's quite
>> handy when you have the same structure repeated but perhaps with
>> different paramater values.
>
>
> The plan for now is to have the system be arrays.  But you could
> pack anything into those arrays.  This is what MCSim and Boost's
> solvers do.  For instance, MCSim doesn't have any matrix or 2D
> array functionality.  Part of what we're trying to think about is
> how critical that'll be.  It probably won't go in our first implementation
> even if we do think it's critical.  We just don't have much time to
> work on this subsystem of Stan.
>
> - Bob
>
>
